prompt: In `type Employee struct { Person; Company string }`, what is the name of the field whose type is `Person`?
hint: How did section 01 set it in the literal?

choices.text: It has none, so only its promoted fields can be reached
choices.why: `e.Person` worked in section 01 and gave the whole inner value; the field has a name.

choices.text: `person`, in lower case, because nobody wrote it
choices.why: The name is the type's name exactly, capital letter included.

choices.text: `Person`, after its type, which is how every embedded field is named
choices.why: Right. An embedded field is named after its type, which is why `Person:` works in a literal.

choices.text: `_`, like any other field without a name
choices.why: `_` is a name you write on purpose to discard something; an embedded field gets its type's name.

prompt: `e` is an `Employee` embedding `Person`. After `e.Name = "Ana Lima"`, what does `fmt.Println(e.Person.Name)` print?
hint: How many `Name` fields does `e` have?

choices.text: The old name, because `e.Name` is a copy of the field promoted into `Employee`
choices.why: Promotion copies nothing; `%+v` showed no `Name` outside `Person`.

choices.text: `Ana Lima`
choices.why: Right. `e.Name` and `e.Person.Name` are one field written two ways.

choices.text: An empty line, since the assignment made a new `Name` at the outer level
choices.why: Assigning never adds a field to a struct; the fields are fixed by the type.

choices.text: Nothing: the short spelling can be read but not assigned to
choices.why: Section 01 assigned through it and the change showed up in `e.Person.Name`.

prompt: The fields of an embedded struct are ___ to the outer struct, which is why `e.Name` finds `e.Person.Name`.
hint: The word section 01 put in bold in the note on `e.Name`.

prompt: A module's `go.mod` says `go 1.26`, and it is built with Go 1.27.1. What happens to `Employee{Name: "Ana", Company: "Acme"}`?
hint: Section 01 ran `go mod edit -go=1.26` and built again.

choices.text: It compiles, since the toolchain doing the build is 1.27.1
choices.why: The toolchain is new enough, but the `go` line sets the language version it compiles, and 1.26 has no such literal.

choices.text: It compiles, and sets a new field `Name` that belongs to `Employee`
choices.why: A literal cannot create fields; `Name` is `Person`'s, reached through promotion.

choices.text: It is refused: a promoted field in a literal requires go1.27 or later
choices.why: Right. The message even ends with `check go.mod`.

choices.text: The go command first downloads Go 1.26 to build it
choices.why: An older `go` line never makes the go command fetch an older toolchain; it compiles with the one it has, as that language version.

prompt: With `type Employee struct { Person; Company string }` and a `go 1.27.1` module, which literals compile? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them mixes the two forms for the same struct.

choices.text: `Employee{Person: Person{Name: "Ana"}, Company: "Acme"}`
choices.why: Yes. The long form names the embedded field and gives it a whole `Person`.

choices.text: `Employee{Name: "Ana", Company: "Acme"}`
choices.why: Yes. Since Go 1.27 a literal can name promoted fields directly.

choices.text: `Employee{Person: Person{Name: "Ana"}, Email: "a@x"}`
choices.why: Refused: `cannot specify promoted field Email and enclosing embedded field Person`.

choices.text: `Employee{Person.Name: "Ana"}`
choices.why: A key in a struct literal is a field name, and `Person.Name` is not one: `invalid field name Person.Name in struct literal`.

prompt: `type Circle struct { Point; Radius int }`, where `Point` has fields `X` and `Y`. What does `fmt.Printf("%+v\n", Circle{X: 1, Y: 2, Radius: 3})` print?
hint: Where do `X` and `Y` really live?

choices.text: `{X:1 Y:2 Radius:3}`
choices.why: That would be true if promotion flattened the struct; it only shortens the spelling.

choices.text: `{Point:{X:1 Y:2} Radius:3}`
choices.why: Right. The literal named promoted fields, but the value still holds a whole `Point`.

choices.text: `{Circle:{X:1 Y:2} Radius:3}`
choices.why: The embedded field is named after its own type, `Point`, not after the outer one.

choices.text: Nothing, because `X` and `Y` are not fields of `Circle` and the literal is refused
choices.why: Before Go 1.27 it would have been refused; in 1.27.1 promoted fields may be named in a literal.

prompt: `greet` takes a `Person`, and `e` is an `Employee` that embeds `Person`. Why is `greet(e)` refused?
hint: Read the error: `cannot use e (variable of struct type Employee) as Person value`.

choices.text: Because Go wants an explicit conversion first, `Person(e)`
choices.why: The conversion is refused as well: the two struct types have different fields.

choices.text: Because `Employee` carries a field, `Company`, that `greet` would not know what to do with
choices.why: Extra fields are not the reason; a struct with exactly `Person`'s fields under another type name is refused the same way.

choices.text: Because they are two different types, and embedding does not make one the other
choices.why: Right. An `Employee` has a `Person` inside it; it is not a `Person`.

choices.text: Because the call needs `&e`, a pointer to the employee
choices.why: A pointer to an `Employee` is not a `Person` either; the types differ either way.

prompt: `e.Name` is `"Ana"`. After `c := e` and `c.Name = "Bia"`, what does `fmt.Println(e.Name)` print?
hint: Where is the `Person` stored?

choices.text: `Bia`, because both employees point at the same `Person`
choices.why: That is the picture of a reference. The `Person` is stored inside the `Employee`, so `c := e` copied it.

choices.text: `Ana`
choices.why: Right. Copying the outer struct copied the `Person` inside it, and `c` changed its own copy.

choices.text: An empty string, since `c := e` moved the person out of `e`
choices.why: Assignment in Go copies; nothing is moved out of `e`.

choices.text: Nothing, as a struct with an embedded field cannot be copied with `:=`
choices.why: It can, and section 02 did exactly this.

prompt: `greet` wants the inner value of an `Employee` called `e`. The call that compiles is `greet(e.___)`.
hint: The embedded field's name.

prompt: `Server`, `Worker` and `Job` each embed a `Logger` struct. You want one function that accepts any of the three. What does Go offer for that?
hint: Section 02 named the half of inheritance that embedding does not cover.

choices.text: A `Logger` parameter, which takes any struct that embeds `Logger`
choices.why: That is exactly the call section 02 saw refused; a parameter of a struct type takes that type only.

choices.text: An interface, the subject of lesson 27
choices.why: Right. Letting different types stand in for one another is what interfaces are for.

choices.text: Nothing: write three functions, one per type
choices.why: Go does have a tool for it; the section points to lesson 27.

choices.text: Converting each value with `Logger(x)` before the call
choices.why: A struct converts only to a type with identical fields, which `Server` is not. `x.Logger` would hand over the part, losing the rest.

prompt: `greet(e.Person)` runs. Inside `greet`, can the code read the employee's `Company`?
hint: What exactly did `greet` receive?

choices.text: Yes, through `p.Company`, because promotion also works upwards
choices.why: Promotion only looks down into embedded structs; a `Person` has nothing above it.

choices.text: Yes, through a hidden link from the `Person` back to its `Employee`
choices.why: There is no such link: the part never learns about the whole.

choices.text: Only if `Company` is exported
choices.why: Exporting decides which packages see a name, not whether a `Person` has a company.

choices.text: No: it has a copy of a `Person`, and a `Person` has no company
choices.why: Right. Nothing inside the part knows it was cut out of an `Employee`.

prompt: `Person` and `Company` both have a `Name` field, and `Employee` embeds both. What does the compiler refuse?
hint: Section 03 points out what was not refused.

choices.text: The declaration of `Employee`, since it holds two fields called `Name`
choices.why: The type compiled; two `Name`s at the same depth are fine until somebody uses the short spelling.

choices.text: Every line that uses `e.Name`, and only those lines
choices.why: Right: `ambiguous selector e.Name`, on the line that uses it.

choices.text: `e.Person.Name` and `e.Company.Name`
choices.why: The long spellings are exact, and they are the fix.

choices.text: Nothing: `e.Name` reads whichever struct was embedded first
choices.why: The order of declaration is never allowed to decide; the compiler refuses instead.

prompt: `Employee` embeds `Person` and `Company`, both with an `Email` field, and declares an `Email` of its own. What does `e.Email` read?
hint: Which of the three is shallowest?

choices.text: `Person`'s, because `Person` is embedded first
choices.why: Order never decides; depth does.

choices.text: Nothing: three fields of one name make `e.Email` ambiguous
choices.why: Only fields at the same depth are ambiguous, and `Employee`'s own `Email` is alone at depth zero.

choices.text: The `Email` declared in `Employee` itself, at depth zero
choices.why: Right. It is at depth zero, shallower than the two inside the embedded structs.

choices.text: `Company`'s, because the last field declared wins
choices.why: Declaration order plays no part in the search.

prompt: `json.Marshal` is given that same `Employee`, whose `Person` and `Company` both have a `Name`. What comes back?
hint: The documentation's third rule ends with `no error occurs`.

choices.text: An error that names the ambiguous field
choices.why: `err` was `nil`; that is what makes this one dangerous.

choices.text: Two `"Name"` keys, the company's after the person's
choices.why: The encoder applies the selector's depth rule and writes neither.

choices.text: An object with no `"Name"` key at all, and a `nil` error
choices.why: Right. Both ambiguous fields are ignored, and nothing says so.

choices.text: A compile error, because the encoder obeys the same rule as the compiler
choices.why: The program never names `e.Name`, so the compiler has nothing to refuse; the encoder works at run time.

prompt: The `Employee` of section 03 embeds `Person` and `Company` and declares `Email`. How many `string` fields does an `Employee` value hold in all, counting the ones inside its embedded structs?
hint: Hidden fields are still stored.

prompt: A program embeds only `Person` in `Employee` and reads `e.Name` in twelve places. Somebody adds `Name string` to `Employee` itself. What happens at the next build?
hint: Compare the depth of the new field with the old one.

choices.text: It compiles, and all twelve now read the new field
choices.why: Right. The new field is shallower, so it wins without a word; this is the direction the rules do not protect.

choices.text: Twelve `ambiguous selector e.Name` errors
choices.why: That happens when the second `Name` is at the same depth, as when a second embedded struct brings one.

choices.text: It compiles, and `e.Name` keeps reading `Person`'s, which was there first
choices.why: Which field came first plays no part; depth decides.

choices.text: The declaration of `Employee` is refused as a duplicate field
choices.why: The two `Name`s are at different depths, and even two at the same depth compile until used.

prompt: Section 03 wrote ``Company `json:"company"` `` in `Employee`. What did the tag change?
hint: Look at where `Acme` appears in the output.

choices.text: It left `Company` out of the JSON
choices.why: That is what the tag `"-"` does; here `Acme` is still in the output.

choices.text: It renamed the company's `"Name"` key to `"company"`
choices.why: The tag is on the embedded field, so it names the whole struct, not one of its fields.

choices.text: The company became an object under `"company"`, so `Name` was no longer ambiguous
choices.why: Right. A named embedded field is not flattened, and `Person`'s `Name` came back.

choices.text: It made `json.Marshal` report the clash as an error
choices.why: Nothing makes the encoder report it; the tag removed the clash itself.

prompt: Put the places `e.X` is looked for in the order the search tries them.
hint: Shallowest first.
items: The fields declared in `e`'s own struct type
The fields of the structs embedded in it
The fields of the structs embedded in those

prompt: For section 03's `Employee` (it embeds `Person` and `Company` and declares its own `Email`), match each expression to what it gives.
hint: Depth first; a tie is an error.

prompt: Which of these are true of an `Employee` that embeds `Person`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are about what is stored and what is promoted; two are about types.

choices.text: Copying an `Employee` copies the `Person` inside it
choices.why: Yes. The `Person` is stored inside, field by field.

choices.text: An `Employee` can be assigned to a variable of type `Person`
choices.why: No. `var p Person = e` is refused just like `greet(e)`; write `e.Person`.

choices.text: A method declared on `Person` can be called on an `Employee`
choices.why: Yes. Methods are promoted like fields; lesson 25 shows it.

choices.text: `json.Marshal` reports an error when two embedded fields clash
choices.why: No. It drops both and returns a `nil` error.
